The leading edge of a trough extending northward from Invest 97W 
(west of Chuuk) is within proximity of the eastern coastal waters of
the Marianas. Gentle to moderate winds have gradually shifted from 
the north to the northeast throughout today, which will become 
easterly on Sunday as the trough moves through the region the next 
couple of days. Increased shower coverage and isolated thunderstorms 
are expected overnight and will peak on Sunday with locally heavy 
showers possible accompanied with gusty winds. Then, southerly to 
southwesterly flow may follow, possibly maintaining speeds of 10 to 
15 mph with scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms at least 
until next weekend.

Marine...
The primary westerly swell from distant Typhoon Bavi (09W) has
remained large enough to induce combined seas hazardous to small 
craft, hazardous surf, and dangerous rip currents along north, south,
and west facing reefs. Altimetry and buoy data indicated sea heights 
between 8 to 10 ft along western coastal waters, so the Small Craft 
Advisory was continued at least through early Sunday morning. The 
westerly swell is expected to relax over the next several days, but 
the long period will keep surf along west facing reefs elevated, 
potentially prolonging the high risk of rip currents beyond Sunday 
morning. However, surf along north and south facing reefs may drop 
below hazardous criteria sometime overnight, so marine conditions 
will be reassessed by 4 AM ChST Sunday. Next week, the primary swell
direction may shift out of the southwest, briefly strengthening, then
maintaining swell heights at least until next weekend.

Tropical Systems...
It's a pretty interesting pattern that we have today, involving a
pair of Invests, a Near-Equatorial Trough (NET), and unusually strong
cross-equatorial flow of 15 to 25 knots. Invest 97W continues to
remain as a "Sub-Low" rating from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center
(JTWC), as does Invest 98W. 97W is currently located near Satawal in
eastern Yap State (near 7.8N 148.1E), and 98 being east-southeast of
Majuro near 5.8N 174.0E. 

Regarding Invest 97W, the models continue to remain in total disarray
regarding if it'll head towards Yap and then off to the northwest, or
will it pass between Guam and Yap doing much the same, or will a new
circulation form east of Guam and absorb some of the energy. The 
next question being, will it develop into a tropical depression or 
stronger? Given the MJO (Madden-Julian Oscillation) is not in phase 
with this wave, significant development is not expected. Instead, 
it'll likely continue to move northwest, passing near or over Guam as
a modestly organized LLCC (Low-Level Circulation Center), while 
remaining below tropical depression strength. Then it'll continue 
northwest on it's journey. Aside from increasing shower and 
thunderstorm potential, residents in Guam and the CNMI can rest easy,
this system isn't expected to be more than a "rain-maker" for us, 
with perhaps an isolated gust or two near 30 mph.

Farther east-southeast, we have Invest 98W by Majuro. This system 
looks less organized than its predecessor, although abundant cloud 
cover and an indifferent scatterometer pass yield little assistance 
in determining LLCC organization/potential. With that said, it's more
convectively active than 97W. This may be an artifact of "better 
preconditioning" from the cross-equatorial flow" The models in
general show this feature moving west-northwest for the next 72 to 
96 hours, before perhaps making more of a west. How much this system 
will organize remains uncertain, as does it's related potential 
strength.

With that said, folks in the Marianas, Yap State, Chuuk, and all of
Eastern Micronesia should continue to monitor these circulations. At
the very least, they'll bring periods of increased rainfall
potential, some of which could be locally heavy. This will be aided
by increased surface convergence near the NET, near the peripheries
of the Invests, and due to the cross-equatorial flow feeding into
these systems. It should be of note, the cross-equatorial flow is a
"wild card in the forecast equation", as the models struggle to
depict how much influence this will have on either systems
development. Thus, to reintegrate, stay informed with forecast
updates, but remain calm as this does not look like a Sinlaku or
Bavi-type event.

Eastern Micronesia...
The cross-equatorial flow discussed in the tropical section above has
really taken hold today, with 15 to 25 knots of south to southwest
winds observed in the scatterometer data and as easily seen in
visible imagery. The interaction of this flow with the pair of
Invests and the NET described above is allowing for fairly expansive
